**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first word was *light*. It slipped out before I could catch it, a whisper lost in the hum of the ceiling fan. I watched it drift upward, dissolving like smoke. Words are strange like that—sometimes they vanish before they’re even heard.

I had 999 left.

II.

I once read that the average person speaks 16,000 words a day. Most of them are forgettable: *pass the salt, I’m tired, what time is it?* But these 1,000 words—these were different. They were a gift, a curse, a dare. What do you say when you know each syllable counts?

III.

My grandmother used to say, *"Words are containers. Some hold love, some hold poison, some hold nothing at all."* She spoke in proverbs, her voice thick with the accent of a village I’d never seen. I wish I’d asked her more questions. Now her words are all I have left of her.

IV.

Word 27: *regret*.

V.

There’s a theory that the universe is made of stories. That every atom, every star, every fleeting thought is just a sentence in some cosmic narrative. If that’s true, then these 1,000 words are my tiny contribution—a footnote, a sigh, a scribble in the margin.

VI.

I tried to write about love once. It came out clichéd and hollow. Love, I decided, is like trying to describe the color blue to someone who’s been blind since birth. You can use all the right words—*sky, ocean, sadness, depth*—but they’ll never *see* it.

VII.

Word 142: *silence*.

VIII.

The most powerful words are the ones left unsaid. The apology you swallowed. The confession you burned. The *I miss you* that died on your tongue. Silence is its own language, heavy with ghosts.

IX.

I remember the first time I understood the weight of a word. I was seven. A boy in my class called me *stupid*. It wasn’t the word itself that hurt—it was the way he said it, like he’d discovered a truth about me I didn’t know. I went home and looked *stupid* up in the dictionary. *"Lacking intelligence."* I cried, not because it was true, but because I feared it might be.

X.

Word 300: *forgive*.

XI.

Language is a living thing. Words evolve, shift, die. *Gay* once meant *happy*. *Awful* once meant *full of awe*. *Nice* used to mean *foolish*. We’re always rewriting the dictionary, one conversation at a time.

XII.

I wonder if animals have words for things we can’t name. Does a dog have a word for the way the air smells before rain? Does a whale have a word for the vast, crushing dark of the deep? What would they say if we could understand?

XIII.

Word 450: *lonely*.

XIV.

The internet is a graveyard of words. Tweets, texts, comments—billions of them, buried under newer ones. We type and type, hoping someone will read, hoping it matters. But most of it disappears, like writing your name in the sand at low tide.

XV.

My father’s last words were *"Turn off the light."* Not profound. Not poetic. Just a man, tired, ready for sleep. I’ve spent years searching for meaning in them. Maybe there isn’t any. Maybe words don’t always have to mean something.

XVI.

Word 600: *enough*.

XVII.

I once loved a person who spoke in riddles. Every conversation was a puzzle. *"The moon is a thief,"* they’d say, and I’d spend hours trying to decode it. Eventually, I realized they weren’t being mysterious—they were just bad at being direct. Some people use words like shields.

XVIII.

The oldest written word we’ve found is *push*, carved into a clay tablet 5,000 years ago. A command. An instruction. A single syllable that outlived empires. What will our words say about us in 5,000 years? *Like. Share. Buy. More.*

XIX.

Word 750: *hope*.

XX.

I’m running out of words. I could fill the rest with grand declarations—*life is fleeting, love is eternal, the universe is vast*—but those aren’t my words to give. They belong to poets, philosophers, people braver than me.

XXI.

So here’s the truth: I don’t know what to say. Not really. I’m just a person with 1,000 words, trying to make sense of the noise. Maybe that’s enough.

XXII.

Word 999: *goodbye*.

XXIII.

(Word 1000 is the space after this. The breath you take before moving on.)
